title: How American Cities Lost Their Movers and Shakers
author: Aaron Renn
summary: Aaron Renn argues that American cities have suffered a structural loss of civic leadership capacity over the past thirty years, driven chiefly by corporate consolidation that turned locally rooted CEOs into branch managers of national and global firms. To make the shift visible he uses Claude to analyse the rosters of Indianapolis's flagship leadership development program, the Stanley K. Lacy Executive Leadership Series, across its eras. The analysis shows the program moving from an elite corporate and professional-services pipeline, which credentialed people who would run the city, to a broader, more diverse, nonprofit-heavy network built around shared values rather than concentrated power. Renn reads this as a proxy for the wider civic leadership class: fewer genuine movers and shakers, more functionaries and stakeholders, and little appetite for the risky, distinctive initiatives that produced Indianapolis's sports strategy. He is careful to say the people are not less competent than before, because the surrounding structure has changed, though he also faults Boomers for failing to develop successors. The piece closes by presenting the method itself, pointing AI at a long list of names, as a newly cheap way to study institutions.
points: The decline of civic leadership is structural: when banks, utilities and retailers stopped being locally owned, the executives whose incentives were tied to their city's growth disappeared from local boards.

A leadership program's roster is a usable proxy for a city's leadership class, and Indianapolis's program shifted from corporate power brokers to nonprofit and government professionals over four eras.

Renn distinguishes a program that aligns power with civic responsibility from one that aligns people who already share civic values, noting the latter is more inclusive but has less leverage over capital.
Big, risky city-defining initiatives need people who can take political and financial risk and induce others to follow, a capacity that more networked, consensus-bound leadership no longer supplies.
Renn says Boomers have been poor at developing and empowering the next generation, preferring loyal soldiers to future generals.
quotes: Today, many CEOs of once-local companies are branch managers of global firms. Their job is to sit on local boards and dabble in community relations, but they don’t really call the shots anymore.

The program has essentially migrated from being a corporate credentialing mechanism — where the Indianapolis business establishment identified its next generation and socialized them into civic responsibility — to something closer to a nonprofit and civic-sector professional development program that happens to include some corporate participants.
Early SKL solved a key problem: “How do we make powerful people care about the city?” Modern SKL solves a different problem: “How do we connect people who already care?” Those are not the same.
There are fewer genuine mover and shaker types today, many more corporate functionaries and non-profit people.
It’s not that the people here are dumber or less competent than they used to be. But the entire economic and civic structure in which they are embedded is different.
Boomers want loyal soldiers in their own army, not to raise up people who might plausibly be generals in their own right some day.
